summary: Defines managed objects for modeling the Link Management Protocol, using network management protocols. It is on the standards track and was later replaced by RFC 4631.

plainLanguage.summary: A standard dashboard for the protocol that checks the links between neighboring optical devices.

questions: how do you manage lmp with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for managing optical link quality and connectivity

tldr.problem: Optical networks need a standardized way to monitor and manage Link Management Protocol (LMP) operations, including control channel connectivity and data link verification.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module with tables for LMP neighbors, control channels, data-bearing links, and performance counters, allowing SNMP tools to read and configure LMP devices.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now manage LMP implementations on optical switches and routers via standard SNMP, monitoring performance and configuring link verification. RFC 4631 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 4327 is a Proposed Standard. It was obsoleted by RFC 4631, which consolidates and extends the LMP MIB specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4327 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the Link Management Protocol (LMP), a protocol that manages traffic engineering (TE) links in optical networks. The MIB module supplies SNMP objects that let network operators monitor and configure LMP on photonic switches, optical cross-connects, and routers.

LMP has four key jobs: maintaining the control channel that carries management messages, verifying data-bearing links are physically connected, detecting link faults, and correlating link properties between network nodes. This RFC exposes those functions as manageable SNMP objects.

The RFC is part of the Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) standardization effort, which treats optical and packet networks with a common control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: LMP is the manager between neighboring optical switches; this RFC gives you a dashboard to watch and control that manager using standard network management tools.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The MIB module rests on several LMP concepts. An LMP adjacency is a partnership between two nodes that agree to exchange LMP messages over dedicated control channels. Several control channels can run at the same time between the same pair of nodes, so if one fails, the other can carry the load.

Data-bearing links (called component links or ports depending on whether they can be bundled) are the actual optical circuits carrying traffic. LMP groups one or more of these into a traffic engineering (TE) link, a logical bundle that the routing system can use as a single link.

LMP can verify that data-bearing links are physically connected by sending test messages, and it detects faults so links can be removed or rerouted.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of control channels as a pair of walkie-talkies between two managers; data-bearing links are the roads they manage; and a TE link is a bundle of roads treated as one.

sections.title: The MIB Tables
sections.content:
The LMP MIB module defines eight main tables, exposed as SNMP objects. The lmpNbrTable lists remote nodes that this node exchanges LMP messages with. The lmpControlChannelTable holds configuration for the control channels between adjacent nodes, including hello interval, hello dead interval (how long to wait before assuming the neighbor is down), and authentication settings.

The lmpControlChannelPerfTable counts control channel traffic per channel: hello messages sent and received, link verification messages, and acknowledgments. The lmpTeLinkTable specifies LMP configuration for TE links, such as whether link verification is enabled. The lmpLinkVerificationTable configures link verification parameters such as the test interval and transport mechanism (payload, overhead bytes, or trace identifiers for SONET/SDH).

The lmpTeLinkPerfTable counts TE link faults and recoveries. The lmpDataLinkTable maps data-bearing links to their remote counterparts by IP address or interface ID. The lmpDataLinkPerfTable counts data link errors and faults detected on each data-bearing link.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables keep track of who your neighbor is, what control channels you have open, what messages flow through them, which data links are bundled into TE links, and counts of problems.

sections.title: Configuration and Management
sections.content:
To set up LMP on a device, an operator first creates an entry in the lmpNbrTable to declare a neighboring node by its IP address. Then entries are added to the lmpControlChannelTable, one for each control channel to that neighbor, specifying the underlying interface, the hello interval and dead interval, and authentication settings.

Next, data-bearing links are created in the lmpDataLinkTable, each tied to an interface and its remote equivalent. For link verification, entries are added to the lmpLinkVerificationTable with the test interval, dead interval, and the transport mechanism for test messages.

Finally, TE links are created as interface entries with type teLink, and LMP-specific configuration is added to the lmpTeLinkTable, specifying whether verification and fault management are enabled.

The MIB module supports both configuration (read-write objects) and monitoring (read-only counters). The RFC notes that access to these objects must be restricted to authorized management systems via SNMPv3 authentication and encryption, since unauthorized changes can disrupt network operations.
sections.plainLanguage: You create a neighbor entry, add control channels, list the data links, say how often to test them, and turn the manager on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB module exposes sensitive network information. Write-accessible objects in the lmpNbrTable, lmpControlChannelTable, lmpTeLinkTable, and lmpDataLinkTable could disrupt network resource allocation if modified without authorization. Read-only objects expose network provider IP addresses and the control and data network topology.

The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic security (authentication and encryption) for all access. Older SNMP versions (SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c) send credentials in the clear and are not recommended. Even on an otherwise secure network, operators must configure SNMP access controls to ensure only authorized users can GET or SET these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: These settings control your network's links, so only trusted people should be able to read or change them. Use the newest, most secure version of SNMP.
